blogs.title: The POD5 Trap: Recognizing Early-Onset HIT After Cardiac Surgery
blogs.description: Early postoperative thrombocytopenia is usually explained by CPB-related dilution/consumption with a nadir around POD2–3 and recovery by POD4–5. This case shows a steady decline from POD1 to POD5 with stroke and a strong-positive PF4 ELISA—classic flags for HIT despite the “too-early” timing. The clincher was a small preoperative UFH exposure during radial cath one week earlier, priming an anamnestic response. We’ll walk through how to differentiate expected CPB thrombocytopenia from HIT in the first week, why even low-dose preop UFH matters, and why continuing LMWH prophylaxis after surgery can perpetuate antigenic drive due to cross-reactivity. Practical pearls: history-taking for recent heparin exposures, when to stop all heparinoids, and how to apply (and adjust) pretest probability thinking in the post-CPB patient.

blogs.title: Autoimmune HIT in the Lab: When the SRA Lights Up at Zero Heparin
blogs.description: Autoimmune HIT (aHIT) features heparin-independent platelet activation—functional assays show robust activation even at 0 U/mL heparin. This case adds a twist: only partial suppression of serotonin release with FcγRIIa blockade (IV.3), creating an “indeterminate” read that could mislead clinicians. We break down SRA patterns for classic HIT vs aHIT, what strong 0-heparin reactivity means, pitfalls of interpreting partial Fc blockade, and when to request expanded platelet activation testing or repeat assays over time. Take-home: a strong PF4 ELISA plus thrombotic complications and 0-heparin activation should push you to treat for aHIT—even if the initial functional report seems atypical.

blogs.title: Argatroban, Fondaparinux, and AT: Building an Anticoagulation Plan for aHIT-Driven Consumptive Coagulopathy
blogs.description: This patient deteriorated biochemically on argatroban (falling fibrinogen, rising D-dimer, new schistocytes)—a phenotype of HIT-associated consumptive coagulopathy seen in severe aHIT. The team pivoted to therapeutic fondaparinux with antithrombin (AT) supplementation for a low AT level, with subsequent stabilization and count recovery. We discuss how to read coagulation biomarkers to gauge control of HIT hypercoagulability, why a short half-life DTI may be preferred immediately post-stroke, when and how to switch to fondaparinux, the rationale for checking AT and administering AT concentrate, and practical dosing/monitoring tips. We also cover alternatives (bivalirudin) and common pitfalls (heparin flushes, underdosing).

blogs.title: IVIG for aHIT: Magic Bullet or Modest Helper?
blogs.description: High-dose IVIG often produces a brisk platelet rise in aHIT by interfering with Fc-mediated platelet activation—but not always. Here, 100 g daily ×2 then a third 100 g dose yielded only a modest bump, consistent with unusually potent antibodies and partial resistance to Fc blockade. We review IVIG mechanisms, dosing strategies, expected time-to-response, and predictors of poor response. We also outline what to do next when IVIG underperforms: ensure robust non-heparin anticoagulation, consider repeat/extended dosing in select cases, and know when to escalate (eg, plasma exchange for pre-op emergencies) while weighing thrombotic and volume/viscosity risks. Bottom line: IVIG supports, but does not replace, effective anticoagulation in aHIT.

blogs.title: Anticoagulating the New Stroke in HIT: Walking the Tightrope
blogs.description: Acute ischemic stroke in HIT with platelets <30×10⁹/L is a management crucible. This case illustrates a rational path: immediate non-heparin anticoagulation with a short half-life DTI (argatroban) to mitigate new thrombosis while closely watching for hemorrhagic transformation, then transition once stable. We cover decision points: timing relative to stroke onset and imaging, platelet thresholds, choosing and titrating a DTI, neuro-monitoring, and mitigating iatrogenic heparin exposures (catheter flushes, line locks). Practical guidance balances hemorrhage risk against the high thrombotic momentum of aHIT.

blogs.title: From Strong ELISA to DOAC: Using Serial Serology to Steer Long-Term Management
blogs.description: PF4 ELISA ODs and functional assays evolve in aHIT. This patient’s SRA remained positive for months, gradually shifting from heparin-independent to predominantly heparin-dependent activation as the immune response waned—mirroring clinical recovery and enabling a step-down to a DOAC (apixaban) after platelet normalization. We outline how to use serial serology to inform ongoing risk assessment, reinforce strict heparin avoidance during the active phase, and plan long-term anticoagulation. Pearls include timing for DOAC transition once stable, communicating a “heparin allergy” plan for future procedures (use argatroban/bivalirudin), and counseling on the natural history of antibody decline.
